embellish.path: French embellir meant to make beautiful, from bellus, pretty. Making something more beautiful with extra ornament shifted to adding extra, sometimes invented, decorative details to a story or object.

emblazon.path: French blason meant a heraldic shield or coat of arms. To emblazon was to paint arms conspicuously on a shield, and the word broadened to displaying anything boldly and conspicuously.

emboss.path: Old French boce meant a knob or protruding bump. To emboss is to raise a design on a surface so it bulges outward like that bump, a design you can feel.

embroil.path: French brouiller meant to mix up or muddle, related to broth being stirred into a murky mix. To embroil someone is to stir them into a confused, conflicted situation.

embroiled.path: From the same root as embroil, embroiled describes the state of having been stirred into a muddled, conflicted situation and stuck there.

embryonic.path: Greek embryon meant something growing or swelling within, from bryein, to swell. An embryo is a life form still developing inside, so embryonic describes anything at that same early, undeveloped stage.

emend.path: Latin emendare meant to free from fault, from mendum, a defect or error. Emend narrowed to the specific act of correcting faults in a written text.

emetic.path: Greek emetikos meant causing vomiting, from emein, to vomit. An emetic is simply a substance whose purpose is to induce that reaction.

eminent.path: Latin eminere meant to stand out or project above others, like a peak rising above a range. Someone eminent stands out above others in distinction and respect.

emissary.path: Latin emissarius meant one sent out, from mittere, to send, the root behind mission and message. An emissary is literally sent forth to represent someone else on a mission.

emollient.path: Latin emollire meant to make soft, from mollis, soft. Emollient describes anything, literally a skin cream or figuratively words or actions, that softens and soothes.

emolument.path: Latin emolumentum originally meant a miller's payment for grinding grain, from molere, to grind. The word broadened from that specific fee to any payment received for holding a position or office.

empathetic.path: Greek empatheia meant feeling into something, from pathos, feeling. Coined in English by analogy with sympathy, empathetic describes the capacity to feel one's way into another person's emotions.

empirical.path: Greek empeiria meant experience, from peira, a trial or test. Empirical came to describe knowledge based on observed trial and experience rather than pure theory.

empiricism.path: From the same Greek root as empirical, empiricism names the philosophical position that all knowledge ultimately comes from sensory experience rather than innate reason.

emulate.path: Latin aemulari meant to rival or strive to equal, from aemulus, a competitive rival. Emulate kept that sense of imitating someone as a model while striving to match or surpass them.

enamor.path: Old French enamourer meant to inspire with love, from amor, love. To enamor someone is literally to put them into a state of love or fascination.

enchant.path: Latin incantare meant to cast a spell by chanting, from cantare, to sing. Magic spells were sung or chanted, so enchant kept the sense of casting a spell, whether literally bewitching or figuratively delighting someone.

enclave.path: French enclave derives from Latin inclavare, to shut in with a key, from clavis, key. An enclave is a territory locked in and enclosed within a larger, surrounding one.

encomium.literal: a song sung in a victory procession
encomium.path: Greek enkomion meant a hymn of praise sung in a komos, a festive procession honoring a victor. Encomium kept the sense of formal, celebratory praise.

encroach.literal: to hook in, seize with a hook
encroach.path: Old French encrochier meant to seize with a hook, from croc, hook. Grabbing bit by bit with a hook became the image for gradually intruding on territory or rights that are not one's own.

encroachment.path: From the same root as encroach, encroachment names the act itself: gradually seizing or intruding on territory or rights bit by bit, as if hooking it in.

encumber.path: Old French encombrer meant to block or obstruct, from combrer, to heap up debris. To encumber someone is to load them down with a burden, a heap that hinders movement.

encyclopedic.path: Greek enkyklios paideia meant the well-rounded circle of learning expected of a free person. Encyclopedic came to describe knowledge or coverage as vast and comprehensive as an entire circle of learning.

endemic.literal: among the people, native to a place
endemic.path: Greek endemos meant native or belonging to a particular people or district, from demos, the people. Endemic describes something that regularly occurs within and belongs to a particular place or group.

endow.path: Old French endouer meant to provide with a dowry, from Latin dotare, to endow, related to dos, dowry. Endow broadened from giving a marriage dowry to providing anyone with any quality, gift, or fund.

endue.path: Latin induere meant to put on, as in putting on clothing, related to ducere, to lead. Endue kept the figurative sense of clothing someone with a quality, investing them with it as if putting it on.

enduring.path: Latin indurare meant to harden, from durus, hard, the same root as duress. To endure is to hold hard against hardship, and enduring describes what lasts a long time, hard and unyielding to time.

enervate.literal: to take the sinew out of
enervate.path: Latin enervare meant to remove the sinews, literally to cut the tendons that give strength. Losing that physical sinew became the image for draining someone of energy and vigor.

enervated.path: From the same root as enervate, enervated describes the resulting state: stripped of sinew and strength, drained of energy and vitality.

engage.literal: to put in as a pledge
engage.path: Old French engager meant to pledge or pawn something, putting it in as a guarantee, from gage, a pledge. Binding oneself by a pledge broadened to occupying, involving, or committing oneself to any activity or conflict.

engender.path: Latin ingenerare meant to beget or produce, from genus, birth or kind. Engender kept that sense of generating or giving rise to something, as if bringing it to birth.

enhance.path: Old French enhaucer meant to raise or lift up, ultimately from Latin altus, high, the root of altitude. Raising something in height extended to raising its quality or value.

enigma.path: Greek ainigma meant a riddle or dark saying, from ainos, a fable or allusive tale. Enigma kept the sense of something deliberately puzzling, whose meaning is hidden like a riddle's.

enigmatic.path: From the same Greek root as enigma, enigmatic describes anything that behaves like a riddle: mysterious, puzzling, and hard to interpret.

enjoin.literal: to join a command onto someone
enjoin.path: Latin injungere meant to impose or attach, from jungere, to join, the root of join and junction. To enjoin is to attach a firm order onto someone, commanding them to do or stop something.

enmity.literal: the state of being an enemy
enmity.path: Old French enemi, enemy, comes from Latin inimicus, not a friend, from in- (not) plus amicus, friend. Enmity is simply the noun for that hostile, enemy-like relationship.

ennui.literal: a state of being annoyed, tired of things
ennui.path: French ennui traces to Late Latin inodiare, to cause hatred or annoyance, related to odium. It narrowed from general annoyance to the specific weary, listless boredom of having nothing to engage one's interest.

enormity.path: Latin enormis meant out of the norm, straying beyond a normal pattern or rule. Deviating from the moral norm gave enormity its sense of monstrous wickedness, distinct from mere enormous size.

enrapture.path: Rapture comes from Latin rapere, to seize or snatch away, the root behind rapid and rapt. To enrapture is to seize someone's mind as if carrying them off, filling them with delight.

ensconce.path: Sconce once meant a small defensive fort or screen. To ensconce someone was to shelter them behind a fortification, and the word settled into meaning to settle comfortably and securely in place.

ensue.path: Old French ensuivre meant to follow, from Latin sequi, to follow, the root of sequence. Ensue kept exactly that: to come after and follow as a consequence.

entertain.path: Latin intertenere meant to hold in a certain state, to maintain. Holding guests or holding an idea in mind led to two senses: to entertain guests by amusing them, and to entertain an idea by considering it.

enthrall.path: Thrall came from Old Norse thraell, a slave. To enthrall someone literally meant to enslave them, and the word softened to mean captivating someone's attention as completely as if holding them in bondage.

entice.path: Old French enticier meant to incite or provoke, probably from Latin titio, a firebrand, the image of kindling a fire. Entice narrowed to tempting someone by kindling their desire with something appealing.

entitled.literal: given a title, a claim to right
entitled.path: Latin titulus meant an inscription or title establishing a claim. Entitled originally meant given a legal title or right, and the modern sense narrowed critically to believing oneself owed privilege regardless of actual right.

entitlement.literal: the state of having a title to something
entitlement.path: From the same root as entitled, entitlement is the noun for a claim or right, and by extension the attitude of feeling owed something as a matter of course.

entomology.path: Greek entomon meant insect, literally something cut into segments, from temnein, to cut, referring to an insect's notched body. Entomology is straightforwardly the systematic study of these cut-up creatures.

entreat.path: Old French entraiter meant to treat or deal with someone, from tractare, to handle. Treating with someone to win them over narrowed to earnestly and humbly asking them for something.

entrenched.path: Old French trenchier meant to cut, the root of trench, a dug ditch. Troops dug into trenches for defense, so entrenched came to mean firmly, defensively established and hard to dislodge or change.
